x.ASV: A Psalm of David. Unto thee, O Jehovah, will I call: My rock, be not thou deaf unto me; Lest, if thou be silent unto me, I become like them that go down into the pit.
x.Darby: [A Psalm] of David. Unto thee, Jehovah, do I call; my rock, be not silent unto me, lest, [if] thou keep silence toward me, I become like them that go down into the pit.
x.KJV: A Psalm of David. Unto thee will I cry, O Lord my rock; be not silent to me: lest, if thou be silent to me, I become like them that go down into the pit.
x.YLT: By David. Unto Thee, O Jehovah, I call, My rock, be not silent to me! Lest Thou be silent to me, And I have been compared With those going down to the pit.

nt: See how you translated this phrase in [18:2](../018/002.md) where it is used with the same meaning.

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not be deaf to me]

David is using **do not be deaf to me** as a common expression of his culture to mean “do not ignore me” or “do not refuse to answer me” (and here it specifically refers to Yahweh answering his prayers for help). If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not ignore my prayers]

Here, **lest, if you are deaf to me, then I will be together with the ones going down to the pit** introduces a possible condition and its consequence. David is saying that if Yahweh does not respond to his prayer, then he will die. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If you are silent, then I will join those who go down to the grave]

David is using **the pit** as a common expression of his culture to mean “the grave” or “death.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the grave]

x.ASV: Hear the voice of my supplications, when I cry unto thee, When I lift up my hands toward thy holy oracle.
x.Darby: Hear the voice of my supplications, when I cry unto thee, when I lift up my hands toward the oracle of thy holiness.
x.KJV: Hear the voice of my supplications, when I cry unto thee, when I lift up my hands toward thy holy oracle.
x.YLT: Hear the voice of my supplications, In my crying unto Thee, In my lifting up my hands toward thy holy oracle.

nt: David is using an imperative form, but **Hear** communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hear]

By **Hear**, David means pay attention to and respond favorably to his request. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Pay attention to]

Here, **voice** represents what David is saying by using his voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Hear the words of my pleas]

Here, **when I lift up my hands** was a symbolic action by which David showed that he was appealing to God for help. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [when I raise my hands in prayer]

By **your inner sanctuary of holiness**, David means the inner sanctuary of the Tabernacle where God dwelled with the Israelites in a special way. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the holy inner sanctuary in your Tabernacle]

Here David uses the possessive form **inner sanctuary of holiness** to mean the inner sanctuary of the Tabernacle that was characterized by holiness. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the most holy place where you dwell] or [your inner sanctuary that is very holy]

x.ASV: Draw me not away with the wicked, And with the workers of iniquity; That speak peace with their neighbors, But mischief is in their hearts.
x.Darby: Draw me not away with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity, who speak peace to their neighbours, and mischief is in their heart.
x.KJV: Draw me not away with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity, which speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief is in their hearts.
x.YLT: Draw me not with the wicked, And with workers of iniquity, Speaking peace with their neighbours, And evil in their heart.

nt: Here **Do not drag me away** is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not drag me away with the wicked]

Here David is speaking of God taking his life as if God were someone who might **drag** him away by force in order to kill him or judge and punish him. See how you translated the similar phrase “Do not gather my soul with the sinful” in [26:9](../026/009.md). If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not bring me away and punish me with the wicked] or [Do not let me die with the wicked]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the wicked, that is, with the workers of iniquity] or [the wicked people who do evil deeds]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase as in the UST.

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and do not drag me away with the workers of iniquity]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ones who do wicked things, the ones speaking of peaceful things with their neighbors]

David is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean evil thoughts or evil intentions. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [while evil thoughts are in their hearts]

Here David is speaking of **evil** as if it were an object that could be located inside people’s **hearts**. The “heart” represents the center of a person’s thoughts and intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while they intend to do evil] or [while they have evil intentions]

x.Darby: Give them according to their doing, and according to the wickedness of their deeds; give them after the work of their hands, render to them their desert.
x.KJV: Give them according to their deeds, and according to the wickedness of their endeavours: give them after the work of their hands; render to them their desert.
x.YLT: Give to them according to their acting, And according to the evil of their doings. According to the work of their hands give to them. Return their deed to them.

nt: David is using the imperative form **Give** to make a polite request to God rather than to give a command. If the imperative form would not communicate a polite request in your language, you could use a different form that would communicate a polite request. [Please give them … please give to them … please return to them] or [I ask that you give them … I ask that you give to them … I ask that you return to them]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Give to them according to their work, yes, according to the evil of their deeds and the work of their hands]

By **their work**, David means the evil deeds and wicked actions of his enemies that he mentioned in the previous verse. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [according to their evil actions] or [according to what their wicked deeds deserve]

Here, **work of their hands** represents the actions that they have done. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to their actions] or [according to what their evil deeds deserve]

By **return to them their recompense**, David means give them the punishment they deserve. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [give them the punishment they deserve]

x.Darby: For they regard not the deeds of Jehovah, nor the work of his hands: he will destroy them, and not build them up.
x.KJV: Because they regard not the works of the Lord, nor the operation of his hands, he shall destroy them, and not build them up.
x.YLT: For they attend not to the doing of Jehovah, And unto the work of His hands. He throweth them down, And doth not build them up.

nt: The implication is that the wicked do not pay attention to or consider what God has done. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they do not pay attention to the works of Yahweh] or [they do not consider the works of Yahweh]
לֹ֤א יָבִ֡ינוּ אֶל־פְּעֻלֹּ֣ת יְ֭הוָה וְ⁠אֶל־מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה יָדָ֑י⁠ו

These two phrases **the works of Yahweh** and **the action of his hands** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [they do not give heed to what Yahweh has done]

David is speaking of God’s judgment as if it is a building **he will tear** down and **not build** up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will destroy them and not restore them]

x.ASV: Blessed be Jehovah, Because he hath heard the voice of my supplications.
x.Darby: Blessed be Jehovah, for he hath heard the voice of my supplications.
x.KJV: Blessed be the Lord, because he hath heard the voice of my supplications.
x.YLT: Blessed is Jehovah, For He hath heard the voice of my supplications.

nt: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless Yahweh] or [I will praise Yahweh]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because he has heard the voice of my pleas, blessed be Yahweh]

Here, **voice** represents the words that David spoke. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has heard my pleas]

Some ancient manuscripts read “for them” and some read **for his people**. For an explanation of the reason why the ULT reads **for his people** see the section in the Psalm 28 Introduction titled “Text variant in 28:8.”

Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **refuge** that provides protection and safety. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and he protects his anointed one like a refuge] or [and he is the one who protects his anointed one]

David is using this possessive form **refuge of help** to mean a place of protection and safety. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and a helpful refuge] or [and a refuge that provides help]

David is using the adjective **anointed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for his anointed king]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, please save your people and bless your inheritance; please be their shepherd and carry them forever]

Here David is speaking of God’s people as if they were his **inheritance**. David is picturing God’s people as something valuable that belongs to God, like property or possessions that are passed down in a family. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your own people]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shepherd** who would guide and protect his people as a shepherd would guide and protect his flock. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [guide and protect them like a shepherd does his flock]

David assumes that readers will know that **unto the eternity** means for all time without end. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for all eternity]
